beats.say: In 1901, divers pulled a lump of green, corroded bronze from a shipwreck. For decades, nobody could explain what was inside it.
It turned out to be a machine of gears, precise enough to predict eclipses years ahead.
It is more than two thousand years old. And nothing as complex is known for at least a thousand years after it.
So who built a computer in the ancient world? And how did it work?
This is the story of the Antikythera mechanism, gear by gear.
Chapter one. The wreck. In early 1900, sponge divers from the Greek island of Symi are working off a tiny island called Antikythera.
About forty-five metres down, they find the sea floor scattered with bronze and marble statues.
It is a shipwreck from the Roman era. Scientists think it sank around 70 to 60 BC.
With help from the Greek navy, the divers haul up treasure through 1900 and 1901. It is one of the first underwater excavations in history.
Among the haul is something nobody pays much attention to: a shapeless lump of corroded bronze and wood, about the size of a large dictionary.
It goes to the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, while the experts focus on the statues.
Then, in May 1902, archaeologist Valerios Stais notices something in one of the broken pieces. A gear wheel, embedded in the rock.
Gears, from an ancient wreck? Many scholars decide it is simply too complex to belong to the ancient world.
And for half a century, the mystery mostly sits in the museum.
Chapter two. The obsession. In 1951, a historian of science named Derek de Solla Price takes an interest.
In 1959, he writes about it in Scientific American, and calls it an ancient Greek computer.
In 1971, he teams up with Greek nuclear physicist Charalampos Karakalos to X-ray the fragments.
For the first time, people can see gears hidden inside the crust. Price counts their teeth, one by one.
In 1974 he publishes Gears from the Greeks. His big find is a gear train, driven by a main wheel that turns once a year.
One gear in that train has 38 teeth. That is two times nineteen. Another has 127 teeth. That is half of 254.
Why those numbers? Because the Moon goes around the sky 254 times in 19 years. The gears are built from astronomy.
But the images are blurry, and the machine is broken into 82 fragments. Much of it stays a riddle.
To read it properly, someone would need to see straight through solid bronze.
Chapter three. X-ray vision. In 2005, the Antikythera Mechanism Research Project brings new tools to Athens.
A British company builds a prototype X-ray machine, just to take 3D scans of the fragments.
Another team uses clever lighting to make faint letters on the surface stand out.
The scans slice through the fragments layer by layer. Gears appear that no one has seen in two thousand years.
So do words. Thousands of tiny Greek letters, hidden under the corrosion, can finally be read.
In 2006, Tony Freeth and colleagues publish the results in the journal Nature. One line of text reads, spiral divided into 235 sections.
The team counts 30 surviving bronze gears, and shows the machine predicted eclipses of the Sun and the Moon.
The style of the lettering points to a machine built in the second half of the second century BC.
So how does a box of bronze gears predict the sky? Let's open it up.
Chapter four. Gear by gear. It all starts with a hand crank on the side. The crank is lost, but its socket survives.
The crank turns the biggest gear, a four-spoked wheel about thirteen centimetres across, designed to turn once a year.
One full turn of the crank moves the date about 78 days. You are winding time forward.
On the front, a pointer runs around a calendar of 365 days. Twelve months of thirty days, plus five extra.
Inside it, a ring shows the zodiac, the band of stars the Sun and Moon travel along, divided into 360 degrees.
The Sun pointer creeps around once a year. The Moon pointer races ahead, going around more than thirteen times.
A little ball on the Moon pointer, half white and half black, turns to show the phase of the Moon.
Now turn the machine around. The back has two big spiral dials, like the grooves on a record.
The top spiral is a calendar. It winds around five times, through 235 months. That is the Metonic cycle, nineteen years.
A pin rides in the groove like a needle, so the pointer follows the spiral outward, month by month.
The bottom spiral is the eclipse predictor. It winds four times, through 223 months. That is the Saros cycle.
After an eclipse, a very similar eclipse comes back 223 months later. That is about eighteen years and eleven days.
Next to certain months sit tiny symbols called glyphs. The 2005 scans found sixteen of them, each one marking an eclipse.
A small dial inside counts three Saros cycles, about 54 years, to correct the hours an eclipse shifts each time.
But the cleverest trick is hidden deeper inside. The Moon does not move at a steady speed.
Its orbit is an ellipse. Near Earth it speeds up, and far away it slows down. The astronomer Hipparchus had a theory for this.
The mechanism builds that theory in bronze. Two gears sit face to face, on slightly different centres.
A pin on one gear pokes into a slot on the other. As they turn, the pin slides in and out along the slot.
So the second gear runs a little fast for half a turn, and a little slow for the other half. The Moon pointer speeds up and slows down, like the real Moon.
And both gears ride on a big gear that turns about once every nine years, tracking how the Moon's orbit slowly swings around.
That is a working model of an astronomical theory, built more than two thousand years ago.
But the inscriptions mention something even more ambitious. The planets. And those gears are gone.
Chapter five. A model of the cosmos. Only about a third of the machine survives, and most of the planet gearing is lost.
In 2021, a team at University College London, led by Tony Freeth, publishes a new reconstruction in Scientific Reports.
Their key clue is an inscription on the front cover. It lists cycles for the planets, including 462 years for Venus, and 442 years for Saturn.
To turn those cycles into gear teeth, the team uses an ancient Greek method described by the philosopher Parmenides.
The result is a display of rings, one inside another, for the Sun, the Moon and the five planets known then, each marked by a little bead.
All of that gearing has to squeeze into a tight space behind the front dial.
Freeth calls it the first model that fits all the physical evidence. Next, the team wants to build it using ancient techniques.
Chapter six. The lost centuries. Here is the strangest part. After this machine, the trail goes cold.
Its makers understood gear trains, astronomical cycles and the theories of Hipparchus. Yet nothing else like it survives from the ancient world.
The closest thing from the centuries after is a much simpler Byzantine geared sundial, from around the year 600.
Machines of similar complexity only appear again in the fourteenth century, in the astronomical clocks of medieval Europe.
That is a gap of well over a thousand years. Whoever built this, their know-how vanished with them.
One corroded lump from a shipwreck proves that the ancient Greeks built a computer of bronze gears to predict the sky.
